definition: Empirical dynamic modeling (EDM) is a framework for analysis and prediction of nonlinear dynamical systems.
details: Applications include population dynamics, ecosystem service, medicine, neuroscience, dynamical systems, geophysics, and human-computer interaction. EDM was originally developed by Robert May and George Sugihara. It can be considered a methodology for data modeling, predictive analytics, dynamical system analysis, machine learning and time series analysis.

explainer.lead: Empirical dynamic modeling, or EDM, is a way to learn about and predict systems whose behavior changes in complicated, nonlinear ways. It turns observed time series into models that can help researchers understand dynamics and anticipate what may happen next.

tiers.eli5: Imagine watching how crowded a playground is each day and using those patterns to guess how busy it will be tomorrow. EDM does something similar for things like animal populations: it learns from earlier measurements instead of assuming the system follows one simple rule. This can help when small changes produce surprising results.
tiers.practitioner: A practitioner applies EDM to observed time series when the goal is data modeling, dynamical-system analysis, or prediction. The workflow is to organize the observations, fit an empirical model of the system's dynamics, and check its predictions against observations. Because the systems are nonlinear, a straightforward extrapolation or a good fit on past data should not be treated as proof that future predictions will be reliable.
tiers.paperLevel: Empirical dynamic modeling is a framework for analyzing and predicting nonlinear dynamical systems from observed data. In plain notation, given observations x(t), the aim is to model the underlying dynamics and estimate future values such as x(t+h). It was originally developed by Robert May and George Sugihara and spans time-series analysis, machine learning, predictive analytics, and dynamical-system analysis.

explainer.example: A researcher records the size of an animal population each month. They use those observations to build an EDM model of the population's nonlinear dynamics, predict the next month's population size, and then compare that prediction with the count actually observed.

explainer.intuition: Some systems do not follow simple, straight-line patterns: the same small change can have different effects depending on the system's state. EDM uses observed behavior to build an empirical picture of those dynamics, rather than relying only on a prewritten equation.
howItWorks: Collect time-series observations of the system being studied.
Use the observations to construct an empirical model of its nonlinear dynamics.
Use the model to analyze relationships in the system's behavior or predict future observations.
Compare predictions with observed outcomes to assess the model.
explainer.whyItMatters: EDM provides a common framework for studying systems whose behavior is difficult to capture with simple models. Its applications range from population dynamics and ecosystem services to medicine, neuroscience, geophysics, and human-computer interaction.
misconceptions: EDM is a framework and methodology, not one application limited to ecology.
An empirical model is not the same as a complete physical explanation of the system.
Nonlinear modeling does not guarantee accurate predictions for every future condition.
